sections.description: John Eske introduces gamutography as the discipline of teaching cameras to adapt to gameplay. He outlines the three main camera styles—fixed-angle third-person, dynamic-angle third-person, and first-person—and notes that camera distance is a central differentiator among them.
sections.title: Intro to gamutography and three camera styles

sections.description: Eske explains that camera design yields many failure modes (there are many more problems than designers can cover in a talk). He uses Journey to illustrate where iterative practice often fixes problems while noting that shipped games still exhibit issues.
sections.title: Problem framing and Journey context

sections.description: The talk introduces maintaining line of sight, handling occluders, and the use of whiskers (ray casts) to detect obstacles early and steer the camera preemptively—balanced against the player's intent to move the camera.
sections.title: Line of sight and obstacle-avoidance basics

concepts: seven DOF (yaw, pitch, roll, offsets, FOV)
sections.description: Eske identifies seven camera degrees of freedom and describes separating constraints by degree of freedom to ensure predictable prioritization—especially keeping the player’s control as a priority over automatic adjustments.
sections.title: Seven degrees of freedom and constraint management

sections.description: This section covers maintaining line of sight with obstacles, handling near clipping, and avoiding abrupt camera cuts. It also discusses how distance and field of view should be coherently driven by pitch to prevent jarring changes.
sections.title: Line-of-sight in dynamic scenarios and non-cut transitions

sections.description: The final portion focuses on scripted camera hints, balancing guidance with player control, multi-input modalities (analog and gyroscope), and accessibility measures to mitigate simulation sickness. Eske stresses testing with diverse demographics and discusses opportunities for tooling (e.g., a potential Unity plug-in) to help teams start from solid camera foundations.
sections.title: Hints, controls, sickness, and practical takeaways

summary: This video presents a focused talk on the challenges of designing third-person game cameras, delivered by John Eske (Backend Company) at the GDC Festival of Gaming. Framed around the idea that cameras reveal failures, Eske formalizes a discipline called gamutography and outlines three core camera styles (fixed-angle third-person, dynamic-angle third-person, and first-person). He enumerates and analyzes dozens of failures that can derail camera behavior, illustrates practical remedies (from obstacle-aware whiskers to near clipping safeguards), and emphasizes maintaining player intent and line of sight. Throughout, he uses Journey as a running case study and interleaves cinematic principles (like the 30-degree rule and rule of thirds) with game-specific constraints (seven degrees of freedom; Separation of concerns). The talk also covers player accessibility (simulation sickness, adjustable field of view, screen shake, and input options) and ends with a practical Q&A on tooling and collaboration across disciplines.
title: 50 Game Camera Mistakes — camera design deep-dive from GDC Festival of Gaming
